notes:
I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could check several of the sites on your list. Nothing here comes from Wesley's Notes, Seedbed, Pneuma Review, the Lutheran sites, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of Job 13. I've left those out rather than guessing. The church labels I give the older commentators (Henry, Gill, Benson and so on) are my own and don't come from the pages.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–2**
- **Guzik:** Job is pushing back on his friends' claim to know more than he does. To them, especially Zophar, the case looked simple, so Job must be missing the obvious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **Matthew Henry:** Those who enter into disputation enter into temptation to magnify themselves and vilify their brethren more than is fit, and therefore ought to watch and pray against the workings of pride. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **NET note:** "I am not inferior" uses the verb "fall," as it was in Job 4:13 to express becoming lower than someone, i.e., inferior. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** This starts a theme that ends in Job all but demanding that God explain his suffering. God's reply fills the book's last chapters. What pushed Job to it was his friends insisting on their wrong answer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **NET note:** "Speak" here means "I desire to speak." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 4**
- **Benson:** The "lies" are false doctrine, namely, that great afflictions are peculiar to hypocrites and wicked men. The friends were bad doctors, prescribing bad remedies: and misapplying good ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-4.htm
- **Barnes:** "Lies" means more broadly sophisms, false accusations, errors. The friends were like doctors called to a sickbed who could do nothing once they arrived. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/job/13-4.html
- **Gill:** "Physicians of no value" can be rendered "idol physicians," no more able to heal than an idol. He applies the verse to Christ as the only physician of the soul. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/13-4.html
- **Henry:** To broken hearts and wounded consciences all creatures, without Christ, are physicians of no value. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **Clarke:** The word for "smear" or "forge" may mean surgeons, giving Ye are CHIRURGEONS of falsity, and worthless PHYSICIANS. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/13-4.html
- **Guzik:** We can feel for Job, but believers are held to a higher standard than this kind of retort (Rom 12:17; 1 Pet 2:21–23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 5**
- **NET note:** Job is rather sarcastic here, indicating if they shut up they would prove themselves to be wise (see Prov 17:28). https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=13&verse=5
- **JFB:** Quotes the Arab saying "The wise are dumb; silence is wisdom." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 6**
- **Henry:** Job begs they would be silent and give him a patient hearing, v. 5, 6. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 7**
- **JFB:** The friends use fallacies to vindicate God in His dealings; as if the end justified the means. Their deceit was claiming Job was a sinner because he was suffering. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **NET note:** Job is amazed that they would say false things on God's behalf. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **Guzik:** The friends acted like God's lawyers but misrepresented him, because what they said wasn't true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 8**
- **NET note:** The idiom is "Will you lift up his face?" this expression usually means that a judge is taking a bribe. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **JFB:** Partiality can never please the impartial God, nor the goodness of the cause excuse the unfairness of the arguments. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 9**
- **Guzik, quoting Smick:** God would judge the friends for their deceit even though they used it in his defence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** The friends' partiality was really toward themselves. They would never want to be treated the way they were treating Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **NET notes:**
  - "Secretly" suggests a guilty act (cf. 31:27).
  - Peake observes that even while Job boldly attacks God's justice, he trusts God's righteousness not to let liars defend him.

  https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **JFB:** God can successfully vindicate His acts, and needs no fallacious argument of man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 11**
- **Henry:** There is in God a dreadful excellency. Job speaks as someone who had himself lived in holy fear, whatever his friends suggested. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **JFB:** The fear in view is fear of using sophisms in God's name. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 12**
- **Guzik:** Their "wisdom" was mere platitudes with no substance, and it left Job feeling burned over. He quotes Morgan: men can argue for God on false lines through limited knowledge and so be unfair without meaning to be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **Henry:** Cites Bishop Patrick's reading that their arguments are no better than dust, and the arguments you accumulate but like so many heaps of dirt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 13**
- **Guzik:** Perhaps the friends tried to interrupt, and Job insisted on finishing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **NET note:** The Hebrew means something like "stand away from me in silence." "Let come… what may" describes misfortune coming against him. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Job+13%3A13%2C19

**v. 14**
- **JFB:** The line is a proverb for "Why should I anxiously try to save my life?" The first image is that of a wild beast, which in order to preserve his prey, carries it in his teeth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 15** (the key verse; see also §2 and §3)
- **Guzik:** This attitude carries Job through his crisis. Job felt God was against him and still said he would trust him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **Spurgeon, via Guzik:**
  - Job's words answer Satan's charge that he served God only because of the "hedge."
  - "Slaying times" show we are God's children, and they create, test and grow faith.
  - Christ fulfilled the verse: he trusted God while being slain.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **Henry:** we must be well pleased with God as a friend even when he seems to come forth against us as an enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/13-15.html
- **Barnes:**
  - "Slay" means physical death only, with no reference to punishment in the future world, or to the death of the soul.
  - The hope word (yachal) properly means to wait with expectation.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/13-15.html and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/13-15.html
- **Gill:** Prefers the margin reading "trust in him" and notes it can also be "hope in him" or "wait for him." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/13-15.html

**v. 16**
- **Henry:** Job didn't expect rescue in this life, but concerning his eternal salvation he was very confident. Since only hypocrites are rejected, and he knew he wasn't one, he concluded he would not be rejected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **NET note:** The fact that Job will dare to come before God and make his case is evidence – to Job at least – that he is innocent. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 17**
- **NET note:** The form is an urgent call to attention ("Keep listening"). Both "word" and "explanation" are Aramaisms. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 18**
- **NET note:** The pronoun is emphatic, "I know that it is I who am right." Some translate "vindicated," looking at how the lawsuit ends. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **Guzik:** Job's defence is not arrogance but a firm hold on reality. God himself had called him blameless (1:1, 8). Guzik adds a caution: some who think they have Job's firmness are only being sinfully stubborn. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 19**
- **NET note:** If anyone could prove sin against him, Job would be silent and die (literally "keep silent and expire"). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Job+13%3A13%2C19
- **JFB:** It is like our "I would stake my life on it". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **Guzik** reads the NKJV wording ("If now I hold my tongue, I perish"). On that reading, the truth was all Job had left, and giving it up would destroy him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**vv. 20–21**
- **NET note:** Job asks that God not use his overwhelming power against him before they argue. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **Guzik, quoting Andersen:** It is God's hiddenness, not Job's, that horrifies him; compare Cain's words in Gen 4:14. Guzik also separates the "dread" Job fears from the proper fear of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **Bible Hub:** "Remove Your hand" recalls God's direct power (Exod 9:3). https://biblehub.com/job/13.htm

**v. 22**
- **NET note:** Job is calling for the court to convene – he will be either the defendant or the prosecutor. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 23**
- **NET note:** Job uses three words for sin: going astray, missing the mark, and open rebellion. Job and his friends agree that great suffering implies great offences, and he wants to know what they are. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **JFB, citing Umbreit:** The singular "sin" means "I am unconscious of a single particular sin, much less many". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **Guzik:** Job allows that he might be wrong. Compare Ps 139:23–24. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 24**
- **NET note:** "Hiding the face" signals withdrawn favour. If God covers his face, it is because he counts Job an enemy, at least this is what Job thinks. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 25**
- **Spurgeon, via Guzik:** Job pictures himself as a helpless autumn leaf blown about. Spurgeon adds that it is a great blessing to be shown one's own weakness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/
- **NET note:** "Chaff" stands for something too worthless to mention. Job is amazed that God would chase something so slight. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **JFB:** Jesus Christ does not "break the bruised reed". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm

**v. 26**
- **Barnes/JFB:** "Write" is a courtroom term for recording a sentence of condemnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-26.htm
- **Henry:** God's aim in writing bitter things is to bring forgotten sins to mind and lead us to repentance. Time does not wear out the guilt of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/13-26.html
- **Guzik and Coffman:** The verse shows Job never claimed to be sinless. Coffman says he only denies gross wickedness as the cause of his suffering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-13.html
- **NET note:** Job's youthful sins seem trifling next to his suffering, and he thinks it unjust if God is punishing him for them. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13

**v. 27**
- **JFB:** Prisoners' feet were held in stocks until the time of execution. The "print" on his soles could come from the stocks or from his disease. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **NET note:** The word could mean fixed "stocks" or "shackles" that let a prisoner move. The parallel line favours shackles. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=13
- **Guzik, citing Bullinger:** The image may come from owners marking the hooves of their animals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-13/

**v. 28**
- **Henry:** Man is like a rotten thing whose decay starts inside itself, and under God's rebuke especially, he is soon gone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **Bible Hub:** In ancient life, moth-eaten wool was an everyday picture of neglect and fragility. https://biblehub.com/job/13.htm

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 15: "I will hope in Him" or "I have no hope"?** This is the only real split I found. It follows the Hebrew text question, not church lines. Two Hebrew words pronounced alike mean "no" or "in him."
- **For the traditional reading:**
  - **Piper (Baptist, desiringgod.org)** admits a real textual problem and avoided building on the verse for that reason. He still concludes the traditional rendering is the right one. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/though-he-slay-me-why-the-silence-on-this-verse
  - **Gill (Baptist)** says the margin reading "seems best." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/13-15.html
  - **Coffman (Churches of Christ)** rejects critics' freedom to emend the text as they like while refusing an emendation that gives one of the great passages in the whole Bible. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/13-15.html
  - **Barnes** has no doubt the "in him" reading is ancient. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-15.htm
- **For "no hope":**
  - **Ellicott (Anglican)** calls the familiar rendering's accuracy very doubtful. He prefers "Behold He will slay me. I have no hope." He still sees living trust in Job refusing to deny his integrity. https://biblehub.com/job/13-15.htm
  - **JFB** says the "not" reading fits best with Job's other "no hope" passages (6:11; 7:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-15.htm
- **A middle reading:** The Pulpit Commentary renders it "wait for him." It cites Canon Cook's view that "not" may be an old spelling of "in him." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-15.htm

**v. 16 and v. 26: different theological framings**
- **Henry (Presbyterian)** takes "my salvation" as eternal salvation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_013.cfm
- **Gill (Baptist)** reads v. 26 through the covenant of grace: Job thought his youthful sins were already forgiven. Gill also allows a reference to inherited corruption of nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-26.htm
- **Benson (Methodist)** puts more stress on punishment for sins committed before I well knew what I did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-26.htm

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (NET notes) on v. 15:** The Kethib is לֹא (lo', "not"), but the Qere is לוֹ (lo, "to him"). NET follows "hope in him." It notes Dhorme's emendation to "I will [not] tremble" and Davidson's "I will not wait" (cf. NLT). https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=13&verse=15

**Jewish tradition and ancient versions on v. 15:** One Bible Hub commentator (the excerpt doesn't name him) says the Mishnah (Sotah) calls the verse undecided, since it can mean "I hope in Him" or "I hope not." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-15.htm

**Catholic (indirect only):** I couldn't reach the Catholic sites, so this is secondhand.
- The Douay-Rheims renders v. 15 with "I will trust in him: but yet I will reprove my ways in his sight." https://biblehub.com/par/job/13-15.htm
- Barnes says the Vulgate renders v. 26 as "thou wishest to consume me with the sins of my youth." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/13-26.htm
